I'm trying to identify whether "y" in a string acts as a consonant or a vowel. Here's what I've got.

 

UPDATED

For consonant: /\s?[aeiou][bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]y[aieou]+|y[aeiou]+[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]|y[aeiou][bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]|[bcdfghjklmnprstvwxz][aieou]+y/g

(This covers all of the following cases: sayyid ayatola arya yara yandex kanye yell yesterday baloney boys way yearning youth year yet yemen)

For vowel: /\s[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]y|[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]y[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]|[^aeiou][bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]+y[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]?|[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]y[^aeiou]|quay/g

(This covers all of the following cases: rhythm cycle pyrrhic dye temporary lyrical rhythmic cyclical zyzzyva by quay crazy lynn classy syssiphus myrtle myth satyr fly syllable)

 

Are there any cases I'm missing? Could these expressions be any more concise?

Edit: yes, these expressions do highlight more than just the Y, but the point of them is to identify whether the Y is a consonant or a vowel, rather than to grab just the Y.
Is there a better way to write these regular expressions?

For the Vowels expression:
The one case I could find that fails were two-letter words (By, My, etc). Changing the + to a ? appears to address that.

I'd add the ignore-case flag as well, to catch "BY" as well as "By".

I also added a \s to that first exclusion block. Just made things a little more readable IMO (but I freely admit that it's petty and has no value for the scenario you've setup).

Wordfinder's list of words that contain a Y has loads of test-case words to use.
The two-letter words were a bit of a pain to incorporate, but I managed eventually. Thanks for the input.

a shorter but less clear way to refer to a consonant is \w(?-i:(?<![aeiou])) the real way to clean this up is a couple of variables so instead of /\s?[aeiou][bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]y[aieou]+|y[aeiou]+[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]|y[aeiou][bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]|[bcdfghjklmnprstvwxz][aieou]+y/g

try

$vv = '[aeiou]'; $cc = '[bcdfghjklmnpqrstvwxz]'; /\s? $vv $cc y $vv+ | y $vv+ $cc | y $vv $cc | $cc $vv+ y/gx

if you like your regex smooshed together, and I do, either a variable to hold the y character or a character class could eliminate the x flag. Or you could use the x flag to comment each case so if you, or anyone else, finds another one then it can be sensibly added.
